description:
What if you could hear the beauty of the universe?

At AlgoRythm, we're turning NASA's breathtaking views of Earth into immersive sound experiences, making the wonders of our planet accessible to those who cannot see them. By blending technology, science, and music, we're giving sight a new language and transforming data into something everyone can experience.

Because the beauty of our universe shouldn't just be seen. It should be heard, felt, and experienced by all.
summary: AlgoRythm is an Earth Information Jukebox: it turns live NASA satellite data into sound you can explore with your ears and your keyboard. Choose one of seven datasets — Arctic sea ice, air temperature, sea surface temperature, rain and snow, severe storms, wildfires or volcanoes — then move a listening point across the real NASA frame. Pitch follows latitude, stereo follows longitude, brightness opens the filter, colour changes timbre and sharp edges become soft accents, while dark or missing data falls quiet. Nothing is a loop: every parameter is computed from the pixels under your listening point. An eight-second Time Machine morphs between two dated sea-ice frames and speaks the measured change: 7.1 to 4.2 million square kilometres between 31 August 1984 and 31 August 2026. Everything is keyboard-operable, captioned and transcribed, with a blindfold mode and a screen-reader mode. It matters because Earth science is published as colour imagery, which quietly excludes blind and low-vision learners from the data itself.
details:
What it does. AlgoRythm lets a person "listen to" a NASA Earth-data image instead of

reading its colour scale. The app requests a real frame from NASA GIBS, analyses it in the

browser, and maps what it finds to a continuous sound field. Moving the listening point —

by mouse, touch or arrow keys — changes pitch, stereo position, filter cutoff, timbre and

accents in real time, so a coastline, a storm eye or a shrinking ice edge becomes an audible

boundary rather than a colour you have to recognise.

How it works. Frames come through one small server-side caching proxy that serves NASA

GIBS imagery and EONET event metadata, so the browser never hits CORS problems and

the demo needs no API keys. Each frame is drawn to an OffscreenCanvas inside a Web

Worker; pixel colour is inverted through NASA's own published colormaps back into

physical values (degrees Celsius, mm per hour, ice fraction), and the analyser builds a 128-

column feature grid of hue, lightness, saturation, edge strength and decoded value. Those

features drive persistent Tone.js voices with smoothed ramps: vertical position sets pitch

quantised to the dataset's musical scale, horizontal position sets stereo and HRTF

placement, intensity sets a lowpass cutoff of 180 x 18^L Hz plus gain, the hue spectrum

crossfades four timbres, Sobel edge strength adds soft percussive accents, and wholeframe statistics shape an ambient bed. Sea-ice extent is computed with area weighting and

a 15 percent concentration threshold. Reverb uses real acoustic impulse responses, a

limiter protects the mix, and narration ducks the music by 12 decibels.

Time Machine. On sea ice and air temperature, one key plays an earlier frame and morphs

to a later one over eight seconds while the listening point sweeps the map. Pitch, cutoff,

gain and timbre are interpolated cell by cell between the two real analyses, so the sound

changes exactly as much as the data does, and the measured result is both displayed and

spoken: 7.1 to 4.2 million square kilometres of Arctic sea-ice extent between 31 August 1984

and 2026 (minus 41 percent), and 16.1 to 17.0 degrees Celsius of mean August air

temperature between 1980 and 2026.

Benefits and intended impact. Blind and low-vision learners, teachers and anyone who

cannot stare at a screen get a genuine way into NASA Earth data rather than a summary of

it. Keyboard-only operation, live captions, a full transcript, an aria-live region, a blindfoldand-reveal mode and a screen-reader mode are built in, not bolted on. The intended

impact is classroom and public use: a teacher can hand one dataset and one listening task

to a mixed-ability class, and a low-vision user can explore the same data independently.

Tools and stack. React and TypeScript with Vite on the front end; Tone.js and the Web

Audio API for synthesis, spatialisation and dynamics; Web Workers with OffscreenCanvas

for pixel analysis; a Node.js proxy with a disk cache; Python for the analysis and narrationbaking pipeline; deployed on Vercel. All imagery, event data and colormaps come from

NASA GIBS, EONET, Worldview and the Scientific Visualization Studio.

What made it creative. The design treats sonification as an instrument rather than an

alarm: a continuous, playable field you can move through, with a jukebox framing that

invites choosing a "track" of the planet. The Time Machine interpolates two real analyses

cell by cell instead of cross-fading two recordings, and blindfold mode asks listeners to

build a mental map before checking it against the picture.

What we considered. Scientific honesty first: the two sea-ice frames come from different

sensors and products, the 1984 polar gap is counted as ice, and the app says plainly that

this is a comparison of two frames, not a trend analysis, with NASA's long-term records as

the authority. We also weighed accessibility (contrast, focus order, reduced motion, no

mouse-only path), demo reliability (cached proxy, no key management), and licensing,

crediting every NASA source and the royalty-free impulse responses in the app and in the

video.
